entries.title: Middle East: No fresh US strikes on Iran for a second day
entries.summary: Two days have passed without any strikes by the US and Iran. Fighting between Yemen's Houthis and Saudi Arabia has added another layer to the complex Middle East crisis. DW has the latest.
entries.content:
Iran

Middle East: No fresh US strikes on Iran for a second day

Published July 26, 2026last updated July 26, 2026

Two days have passed without any strikes by the US and Iran. Fighting between Yemen's Houthis and Saudi Arabia has added another layer to the complex Middle East crisis. DW has the latest.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • US has not hit Iran for a second day after a nearly-two week streak of nightly strikes
  • Iran has also not announced any new attacks
  • The Middle East war which spread to the Red Sea this week, has also reached the Caspian Sea with Tehran accusing Ukraine of a deadly attack on its vessel.

Here are the lastest developments concerning the Iran war and the wider Middle East on Sunday, July 26.

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Another silent night as US reports no attacks against Iran

Another silent night as US reports no attacks against Iran

No US strikes were reported on Iran on Saturday and Sunday after the US military mounted a 13-night volley of escalating bombardments.

There were also no reports of attacks by Iran on its Gulf neighbors.

The silence is resuscitating hopes of the two sides returning to the negotiation table with the war between them reaching the five-month mark on July 28.

The US military did not announce any new strikes on Sunday but said that a "naval blockade against Iran remains in full effect."

It is not immediately known why the US is holding fire against Iran.

US President Donald Trump, on Thursday told US news-outlet Axios that he was mulling "a massive attack" on Iran which he described as being "bigger than ever before".

But he also says that talks with Iran are pressing ahead.

"We're talking to them right now. I think they're getting more and more serious," Trump told journalists on Friday, adding that Tehran faces a choice between a deal and strikes at a "much higher level".

The US President "has always been clear that his preference is diplomacy, but he has shown Iran what will happen ​if they fail to come to the table in a serious way," Reuters quoted , a senior official in Trump's administration.

Stockpile pressure?

The lull in attacks also comes as US media reports concerns over depleting munitions in the expanding conflict.

CNN cited a US official as saying that Vice President JD Vance and Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Dan Caine both raised concerns about the US defense stockpile with Trump during a White House meeting on Friday.

The official told CNN that Washington’s operations against Tehran were "on a hold.

While the US and Iran are holding back, retaliatory strikes between Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels and Saudi Arabia have opened a new front in the Middle East war.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

The US has seemingly hit a pause button as the Iran war comes closer to completing its fifth month.

Iran woke up to another day without US airstrikes after 13 consecutive nights of an intensified bombing.

Meanwhile, the war has spread to new waters — the Red Sea and the Caspian Sea.

But first, here is a recap of how the Middle East war has fared over the weekend:

  • Yemen's Houthi rebels fired missiles and drones at Saudi Arabia in retaliation to Saudi strikes on the Yemeni port city of Hodeida, which the Iran-backed rebel group holds.
  • Saudi Arabia's strikes were the kingdom's response to the Houthis attacking its tankers in the Red Sea amid a maritime blockade.
  • Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy alleged that Russia was giving Iran satellite data to help direct attacks in the Middle East.

Stay with us for more updates.

entries.title: Vietnamese vessel sinks in South China Sea, 23 missing
entries.summary: A Vietnamese-registered cargo ship carrying 62 crew members sank near Yongshu Reef in the South China Sea, one of the world's most important and contested maritime spaces.
entries.content:
China

Vietnamese vessel sinks in South China Sea, 23 missing

July 26, 2026

A Vietnamese-registered cargo ship carrying 62 crew members sank near Yongshu Reef in the South China Sea, one of the world's most important and contested maritime spaces.

Rescuers were searching on Sunday for 23 people, missing after a Vietnamese ship sank in the South China Sea, China's ⁠state media reported.

Authorities in the Chinese island province of Hainan said the cargo vessel Khoi ​Nguyen 18 ran into trouble near Yongshu Reef, also known as Fiery Cross Reef, state broadcaster CCTV said.

The ship was carrying 62 crew members, and 39 people were rescued from the water.

What we know about the sinking incident

A Chinese rescue ship, the Nanhai Jiu 115, first spotted what was believed to be a distress flare from the vessel shortly before 6:30 pm on Saturday (1030 GMT).

The Khoi Nguyen 18 is a Vietnamese-registered ship measuring just under 70 meters (230 feet) in length, according to state news agency Xinhua.

It added that six Chinese vessels, a rescue helicopter and a Vietnamese vessel were involved in the search-and-rescue operations.

Territorial disputes in South China Sea

Beijing claims sovereignty over almost the entire South China Sea, despite the 2016 international ruling, initiated by the Philippines against China, that its assertion has no legal basis.

One of the most highly contested areas is the ​Spratly Islands, which China calls the Nansha Islands, where China has built runways ⁠and militarized artificial islands.

But ​Beijing's sweeping claims to the busy waterway overlap with those of other countries, including Vietnam, the Philippines, Brunei, Malaysia and Taiwan.

Edited by: Kieran Burke

entries.title: Berlin CSD: Latest in string of deadly vehicle attacks
entries.summary: The attack at a Berlin Pride event is only the most recent incident on a long list where vehicles were used as weapons. The US, Canada, and China also saw similar attacks in recent years.
entries.content:
CrimeGlobal issues

Berlin CSD: Latest in string of deadly vehicle attacks

July 26, 2026

The attack at a Berlin Pride event is only the most recent incident on a long list where vehicles were used as weapons. The US, Canada, and China also saw similar attacks in recent years.

Berlin, Germany, July 25, 2026

A Christopher Street Day event in the German capital, which attracts thousands of people every year, was attacked on Saturday night by a 21-year-old suspect who police said was associated with the "Islamist scene" in Berlin. One person was killed and another 16 people were injured, while the suspect, named as Abdul B., fled the scene.

Leipzig, Germany, May 4, 2026

Two people were killed and 20 more injured in early May when a car drove through a crowd in the eastern German city of Leipzig. The suspect in the case was described as a 33-year-old German national and local resident, who had been known to police, though not for relevant offenses.

Mannheim, Germany, March 3, 2025

At least two people were killed and several were injured in the southwestern German city of Mannheim in 2025 when a motorist intentionally drove his car into a crowd of people, according to police and public prosecutors. Authorities identified the suspect as a 40-year-old German man. Law enforcement ruled out a political motive at the time, though the man had paid a fine under Germany's hate crime laws for a comment he made on a social media platform in 2018.

Munich, Germany, February 13, 2025

A 37-year-old woman and her two-year-old daughter were killed in Munich in February last year when a car was rammed into a demonstration organized by the trade union Verdi. A 25-year-old Afghan man subsequently went on trial for their murder, as well as the attempted murder of the dozens of other people injured in the attack. 

New Orleans, United States, January 1, 2025

A vehicle plowed into a crowd of New Orleans revelers early on New Year's Day 2025, killing at least 10 people and injuring dozens of others. The driver of the vehicle and two police officers were killed in a firefight soon after the attack, which took place at about 3:15 in the morning local time. The FBI said it was investigating the incident as an act of terrorism.

Magdeburg, Germany, December 20, 2024

At least six people died and more than 300 were injured when a man slammed a rented BMW SUV into a Christmas market in eastern Germany. The suspect, who was arrested at the scene, was a 50-year-old doctor originally from Saudi Arabia who had expressed anti-Muslim views and support for the far-right AfD party.

Zhuhai, China, November 11, 2024

A 62-year-old driver rammed a small SUV into people exercising at a sports complex in southern China on November 11, 2024, killing 38 people in the country's deadliest act of mass homicide in years. Another 48 were injured. Authorities said the perpetrator was upset about his divorce but offered few other details about his motive. The man was detained and sentenced to death, and executed in January 2025.

London, Canada, June 6, 2021

Four members of a Muslim family who were out for a walk were killed when an attacker hit them with a pickup truck in what then Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau called "a terrorist attack, motivated by hatred." The 23-year-old white nationalist attacker was sentenced to life in prison.

Toronto, Canada, April 23, 2018

A 25-year-old Canadian man drove a rented van into mostly female pedestrians on the main thoroughfare in Toronto, killing 10 people and injuring 16. He told police he belonged to the online "incel" community of sexually frustrated men. He was sentenced to life in prison with no possibility of parole for 25 years.

New York, United States, October 31, 2017

An Uzbek national killed eight people and seriously injured 12 others when he swerved a rented pickup truck on a bike path in New York City. Reportedly spurred on by a call to action by militant group "Islamic State," he was sentenced to eight consecutive life sentences plus an additional 260 years in prison.

Barcelona, Spain, August 17, 2017

A man driving a van plowed into people on the Spanish city's crowded Las Ramblas boulevard, killing 14 and injuring many more.

The "Islamic State" claimed responsibility, with members of the same cell carrying out a similar vehicle attack in the nearby resort town of Cambrils before being shot dead by police.

The perpetrator of the Ramblas attack was killed by police on August 21 after spending several days on the run.

Charlottesville, United States, August 12, 2017

A white supremacist intentionally drove his car into a crowd of protesters who were opposing a "Unite the Right" rally, killing one woman and injuring dozens of people. He was sentenced to life imprisonment without the possibility of parole.

London, United Kingdom, March to June, 2017

The year 2017 saw a spate of vehicle attacks in the British capital starting on March 22, when a 52-year-old UK-born man rammed an SUV into people on Westminster Bridge, killing four before stabbing a policeman to death. The perpetrator — who was a convert to Islam — claimed to be waging jihad in revenge for Western military action in Muslim countries. He was shot dead.

On June 3, three Islamist attackers drove a van at pedestrians on London Bridge before stabbing people at the city's Borough Market. Eight people were killed and police killed the attackers.

Later that month, on June 19, a 47-year-old man radicalized by far-right ideas drove a van at worshippers outside a mosque in London's Finsbury Park area, killing one man and injuring 15 people.

Melbourne, Australia, January 20, 2017

Six people were killed and more than 30 injured when a car hit lunchtime crowds at a pedestrian mall in Australia's second-largest city. The perpetrator was found to have been in a state of drug-induced psychosis.

Berlin, Germany, December 19, 2016

A rejected asylum-seeker from Tunisia drove a hijacked truck into a Christmas market in the German capital, killing 13 people and injuring dozens. The attacker was killed days later in a shootout in Italy. The attack was claimed by the "Islamic State" militant group.

Nice, France, July 14, 2016

A Tunisian-born French resident drove a rental truck for nearly 2 kilometers along a seaside promenade crowded with tourists. The attack on the French Riviera resort, which took place on France's Bastille Day holiday, killed 86 people — the deadliest of its kind.

(AFP, AP, dpa, Reuters)

This article was first published on April 8, 2025, and updated on July 26, 2026.

entries.title: India news: Home minister backs Pradhan after resignation
entries.summary: Hours after India's education minister resigned amid youth protests, India's home minister spoke out in his defense. Meanwhile, Cockroach party's leader thanked 'cockroaches' across India. DW has more.
entries.content:
India

India news: Home minister backs Pradhan after resignation

Published July 26, 2026last updated July 26, 2026

Hours after India's education minister resigned amid youth protests, India's home minister spoke out in his defense. Meanwhile, Cockroach party's leader thanked 'cockroaches' across India. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Indian Home Minister Amit Shah says youth and students more important for BJP than any post
  • India has a new education minister in Bharatiya Janata Party veteran Prahlad Joshi
  • Cockroach Janta Party's founder says party has 'a long way to go'

Here are the biggest headlines from India on Sunday, July 26:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Scenes from the protest site, late last night

Scenes from the protest site, late last night

At about 8:30 p.m. on Saturday evening, the Cockroach protest site at Jantar Mantar, New Delhi was dwelling in residual euphoria.

Hours earlier, the education minister had resigned and soon after the protest had been concluded. The instant celebration had been loud. Now, many had left, some remained and others walked in.

For some working youths, who had been banking on the weekend to show their support, the news of Pradhan's resignation came a little too early. Robbed of their chance to be a part of the movement, they had decided to witness the last of the celebrations.

At one end of the site, volunteers dismantled the stage where activist Sonam Wangchuk had been on hunger strike for over 20 days. It was the same stage where students sat in protest when Wangchuk had been removed without his consent, where CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke broke down in tears and where he first heard word on Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation.

A few meters away, people formed little circles around those who still danced in celebration. On the sides, protesters with witty placards proudly posed for those taking pictures, showing their creativity once more before putting it away.

Beyond the barricades, some congratulated strangers with water, words or hugs. Others leaned over ice cream carts which had finally made their way in.

And about two hundred volunteers still worked tirelessly, either to control the celebrating crowd, to show people the way out or to sweep the roads. Once in a while their eyes met, and a smile broke out on their faces.

Skip next section "Cockroach Janta Party has a long way to go," says Dipke

"Cockroach Janta Party has a long way to go," says Dipke

A day after the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) ended its 36-day protest in central Delhi, founder Abhijeet Dipke said he finally slept a full night's sleep without worry and panic.

The protest was concluded on Saturday evening after a round of talks between the government and CJP spokespersons. At this time, the government had accepted all of the party's core demands including education minister Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation over exam paper leaks.

"What I went through in the last 37 days was really, really difficult. It was not easy, not just for me, but for all of our team," Dipke said.

The youth leader was recently diagnosed with typhoid, over a month after he camped at the historical protest site of Jantar Mantar with other "cockroaches," in the middle of India's monsoon season.

Dipke thanked protesters across the nation for making the movement a success. He also thanked his critics who questioned the satirical party's abilities and methods. The 30-year-old said the critics had helped the CJP improve.

"Cockroach Janata Party has a long way to go, and for sure we will go a long way. This is just the beginning. Jai Hind," he said.

Skip next section WATCH: Education minister concedes to 'Cockroach' demands, resigns

WATCH: Education minister concedes to 'Cockroach' demands, resigns

India's Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned after nationwide youth-led protests over alleged irregularities in major exams.

Demonstrators organised by the social media-driven Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) demanded education reforms, compensation for affected students and the withdrawal of cases against protesters.

After renewed talks, the government accepted the group’s demands, prompting CJP to end the demonstrations. The protests have been one of the most significant challenges to Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s administration since the 2021 farm protests.

Skip next section Pradhan's 'tenure is a testament to his dedication' says Home Minister Amit Shah

Pradhan's 'tenure is a testament to his dedication' says Home Minister Amit Shah

India's Home Minister Amit Shah defended fellow party leader Dharmendra Pradhan in a social media post hours after he resigned as India's education minister, giving in to nationwide youth led protests.

"For BJP workers, the country, our youth, and students are far more important than any position. Today, the resignation of Union Education Minister Shri Dharmendra Pradhan ji from his post exemplifies this very principle," Shah said on X.

"The Modi government respects the sentiments of the country's youth and is committed to implementing the necessary reforms against paper leaks," he said adding that the government's upcoming legislature to strengthen anti-paper leak laws would help ensure "complete justice."

Shah went on to count Pradhan's "reforms" as education minister. "His efforts toward making the examination system more inclusive and student-centric have also been noteworthy. His tenure is a testament to his dedication to the resolve of making India a developed nation," he said.

Shah's post was one among many from the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party leaders which highlighted similar intiatives and Pradhan's "integrity."

In his resignation announcement on Saturday, Pradhan said he had acknowledged responsibility of the medical entrance exam's paper leak from the very first day.

He said was now resigning because he did not want "anti-national forces" to take advantage of the situations and wanted the youth to once again focus on their education and careers.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Hello and welcome to DW's India blog!

This is Mahima Kapoor, reporting from a cloudy New Delhi where the slowness of the Sunday is both welcome and needed after a week of fiery protests ending in a key resignation. 

Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan gave up his post on Saturday afternoon under pressure from India's Cockroach movement and youth-led protesters over national exam paper leaks.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party has defended Pradhan's efforts and integrity towards his work and the nation.

The government was also quick to install a veteran and low-profile leader Prahlad Joshi in Pradhan's place.

With their core demands met, the Cockroach Janta Party leaders and youth "cockroaches" have vacated the protest site in central Delhi which was cleaned and sanitized overnight. 

Most people have one question on their minds — What's next? Be it for India's education system, CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke or India's Generation Z which is enjoying mass popularity among masses right now.

Stay tuned!

entries.title: Germany launches manhunt after Berlin Pride van ramming
entries.summary: Police believe the 21-year-old suspect, named as Abdul B., has links to the Islamist scene. One person was killed and several others injured in the attack. Follow DW for more.
entries.content:
Published July 26, 2026last updated July 26, 2026

Police believe the 21-year-old suspect, named as Abdul B., has links to the Islamist scene. One person was killed and several others injured in the attack. Follow DW for more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Manhunt launched after deadly van ramming during the Pride event in central Berlin
  • One person was killed, 16 others injured
  • Several people are in a life-threatening condition in hospital
  • Police name suspect as 21-year-old Abdul B.
  • Police said the suspect is known for links to the Islamist scene
  • The Pride parade, celebrating the LGBTQ+ community, is known as Christopher Street Day in Germany
  • The remaining Pride events were called off

Follow DW's coverage for the latest developments on the manhunt and reaction to Saturday night's attack.

Skip next section Berlin Pride atrocity an attack on 'entire country,' says lawmaker

Berlin Pride atrocity an attack on 'entire country,' says lawmaker

Germany's Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said he was "deeply shaken" by the Berlin Pride car ramming, calling it a "heinous attack on people celebrating peacefully."

"My thoughts are with the victims, their families, and everyone who had to witness this act," Dobrindt said in a statement.

"We will do everything in our power to quickly solve this terrible crime and the circumstances behind it and to punish the perpetrators."

Britta Hasselmann, the parliamentary group leader for the environmentally-friendly Green Party, labeled the ramming "an attack on the entire country, on our free and liberal constitutional state and everything that defines it."

One of the hosts of the Pride event, presenter and comedienne Ricarda Hofmann, described being "at a loss for words" following the atrocity.

"I was at CSD today," Hofmann wrote on social media, referring to Christopher Street Day, the name used in Germany to mark Pride events.

"Not just as a presenter, but as part of a community that comes together to be visible. To celebrate love. To stand up for one another."

Pride cohost Jochen Schropp, an actor and presenter, lamented how the day turned into a nightmare.

"It was such a beautiful day, full of love. (...) It was truly indescribable. And then something like this happens. I hope we somehow get through this as a community," he wrote on Instagram.

Skip next section More on the search for Berlin Pride attacker

More on the search for Berlin Pride attacker

The suspect in the  Berlin Pride ramming is known to police and was only released from juvenile detention in May, DPA news agency reported.

Bild newspaper said state security has "extensive information" on 21-year-old Abdul B, related to "religious ideology" and links to radical Islam.

Bild said police commandos stormed a property in Berlin's Schöneberg district overnight, but left without making arrests.

The mass circulation daily also reported that Abdul B. likely rented the white Citroen SpaceTourer used in the attack in his own name.

Meanwhile, the manhunt has been extended to Germany's borders, Bild said.

The newspaper said authorities in the neighboring Netherlands, Belgium, Luxembourg, France, Austria, Switzerland, the Czech Republic, Poland and Denmark have been alerted.

Skip next section Police probe reports of Pride visitors being stabbed

Police probe reports of Pride visitors being stabbed

Berlin police said they were investigating whether the Pride ramming attack had a second phase.

A police statement naming the suspect also noted reports that several people were injured with "stabbing weapons."

Police spokesman Florian Nath cited eyewitness accounts of multiple people suffering stab wounds.

Nath said others described seeing a man dressed in black carrying a machete, DPA news agency reported.

Police are also investigating whether more than one person was seen leaving the vehicle after the ramming attack, AFP news agency reported.

Fire brigade spokesman Dominik Pretz said three of the 16 injured people suffered life-threatening injuries and eight were seriously injured.

Skip next section Merz condemns 'heinous' Berlin Pride van ramming

Merz condemns 'heinous' Berlin Pride van ramming

Germany's  Chancellor Friedrich Merz condemned Saturday night's deadly van ramming at Berlin Pride celebrations, describing it as a "heinous act."

"What a heinous act in Berlin. Hundreds of thousands of people from all over the world were peacefully celebrating at Christopher Street Day. They wanted us to treat each other with kindness and tolerance. This is an attack on our society," Merz wrote on X.

The chancellor added: "The act will be investigated and pursued with the utmost severity."

Meanwhile, Berlin Mayor Kai Wegner, who visited the scene, described the incident as "an attack on our free and open society."

"After a peaceful and colorful CSD, the assembly for a tolerant and peaceful Berlin was attacked in the most brutal way. Berlin is the city of freedom, and our freedom has been attacked in the most horrific way today," Wegner wrote on X.

In remarks to reporters at the scene, Wegner said, "We will not allow our way of life and our way of living together to be taken from us."

Skip next section Germany's history of vehicle rammings

Germany's history of vehicle rammings

Germany has witnessed several deadly vehicle rammings at major public events in recent years.

In 2016, a Tunisian-born man drove a truck into a Christmas market in Berlin, killing 12 people, in the deadliest Islamist attack in Germany's postwar history. A 13th victim later died from their injuries.

In 2024, a man plowed his car into a busy Christmas market in the city of Magdeburg, killing at six people and injuring more than 300 others. The perpetrator was a Saudi-born atheist who held anti-Islamic and far-right beliefs.

Earlier this year, two people were killed after a man drove a car through a crowd in the eastern city of Leipzig. Investigators treated the incident as a rampage and the suspect, a German national, was remanded to a psychiatric hospital.

Skip next section Police name suspect, reports of several stabbed

Police name suspect, reports of several stabbed

Berlin Police named 21-year-old Abdul B. as the suspect in Saturday night's van ramming attack at the Berlin Pride festivities.

In a statement, police described him as of slim build, around 1.9 meters tall, with black hair.

The suspect was wearing a black hoodie and white pants.

Police said Abdul B could be "armed and dangerous" and should not be approached.

The public is advised to call the police emergency hotline 110 if they know anything.

Police also said they were investigating reports that several people were injured with "stabbing weapons," without giving further details.

Skip next section What we know about the attack

What we know about the attack

Good morning from Germany, which is still reeling from Saturday night's van ramming attack at the Pride festivities in Berlin.

One person was killed and at least 16 others injured, authorities said.

Police said a white van had driven into the Tiergarten park around 10 p.m. local time (20:00 UTC/GMT).

The van hit several people before colliding with a tree.

Berlin police said they are linking the attack with the Islamist scene.

Police said they have identified a suspect, named as Abdul B, who is yet to be apprehended.

If seen, the public is advised not to approach him and to call the police.

In a statement, Chancellor Friedrich Merz said he and the country's interior minister would ensure "this horrific act is fully investigated and punished."

Berlin Mayor Kai Wegner denounced the "attack on our free and cosmopolitan society."

The city of Berlin has activated a crisis hotline for people missing friends or family members.

Pride is known as Christopher Street Day in Germany, named after the New York street where the 1969 Stonewall riots began and sparked the modern LGBTQ+ rights movement.

entries.title: Brazil denies entry to senior Trump officials ahead of elections
entries.summary: Brazil rejected visas for two planned US envoys, alleging that Washington was seeking to shape Brazil's upcoming presidential election. The development adds to a deepening political tension between Brazil and the US.
entries.content:
Brazil

Brazil denies entry to Trump officials ahead of elections

July 26, 2026

Brazil rejected visas for two planned US envoys, alleging that Washington was seeking to shape Brazil's upcoming presidential election. The development adds to a deepening political tension between Brazil and the US.

Brazil has denied visas to two officials from United States President Donald Trump's administration who had sought to travel to the country to meet with electoral authorities ahead of the October presidential election.

A spokesperson for Brazil's foreign office said on Saturday that Assistant Secretary Riley M. Barnes from the ​US State Department's Bureau of Democracy, Human Rights, and Labor, had requested a visa on July 20, along with Samuel Samson, a deputy assistant secretary.

The delegation's visa request was rejected on Friday, the spokesperson said.

What has Brazil said?

The Washington Post had first reported on the planned visit of the two envoys, citing senior Brazilian officials who said they had learnt of a US "ploy" that was "completely incompatible with Brazilian democracy."

The denial of the visas was ‌based on "evidence pointing to a renewed attempt to politically exploit the situation and undermine the electoral system", news agency Reuters quoted a Brazilian official as saying.

What has Washington said?

The US State Department said later on Saturday that Barnes and Samson planned to go to the South American country's capital, Brasilia from July 27 to 30 to discuss "election integrity," religious freedom and freedom of expression with government officials, religious leaders and others.

The Associated Press quoted the department as saying that the visit was routine and "any insinuation of a 'ploy' to undermine a democratic nation's election is a baseless lie."

Brazil gears up for elections

Brazil's presidential election is slated to be held on October 4.

President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva is seeking reelection against Flavio Bolsonaro, son of Brazil's former President Jair Bolsonaro.

The right-wing Liberal party confirmed Flavio as their candidate for the presidential race on Saturday.

The senior Bolsonaro, Jair, is under house arrest as he serves a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after his defeat to Lula in the 2022 election.

The former Brazilian leader had also presented unsubstantiated allegations that his country's electronic voting system was vulnerable to fraud.

Flavio recently repeated some of his father's claims.

Bolsonaro-Trump ties

Jair is a friend and ally of Trump and the Bolsonaro family has ties with the Trump administration.

In May, Flavio and his brother Eduardo had visited US officials in Washington, including Trump.

The Trump administration classified two of Brazil's largest drug-trafficking groups as foreign terrorist organizations, in a move opposed by Lula.

Jair was dubbed "Trump of the Tropics" during his tenure.

Trump had railed against Jair's trial, deeming it a "witch hunt".

Edited by: Kieran Burke

entries.title: Berlin: 1 dead, 16 injured after car ramming at CSD Pride event
entries.summary: A citywide manhunt is underway after a van drove into a crowd during Pride celebrations, known locally as Christopher Street Day (CSD). Police have identified a suspect tied to Berlin's "Islamist scene."
entries.content:
Germany

Berlin: 1 dead, 16 injured in car ramming at CSD Pride event

Published July 25, 2026last updated July 26, 2026

A citywide manhunt is underway after a van drove into a crowd during Pride celebrations, known locally as Christopher Street Day (CSD). Police have identified a suspect tied to Berlin's "Islamist scene."

What you need to know

  • 1 person was killed and 3 people suffered life-threatening injuries after a van drove into a crowd at one of Europe's biggest LGBTQ+ Pride events
  • Police have identified a suspect associated with 'the Islamist scene in Berlin'
  • The suspect is named as 21-year-old Abdul B.
  • No arrests have been made, but a manhunt has been launched and more than 2,200 personnel have been deployed as part of the police operation
  • The area around the Tiergarten park in central Berlin has been closed off

At least one person has died and 16 people were injured, "some seriously", police said, after a vehicle was driven into a crowd near Berlin's annual Pride event, Christopher Street Day (CSD) on Saturday night.

"We believe that a vehicle entered the Tiergarten park and hit several people," police said on social media.

Berlin's CSD is one of Europe's biggest Pride events celebrating the LGBTQ+ community. It attracts tens of thousands of visitors from around the world each year.

What do we know about the alleged attacker?

Police spokesperson Florian Nath said a suspect has been identified who was known to police and "is believed to be associated with the Islamist scene in Berlin."

In a later statement, police named 21-year-old Abdul B. as the man they are hunting, describing him as of slim build, around 1.9 meters tall, with black hair. He was wearing a black hoodie and white pants.

Police said the suspect could be "armed and dangerous" and should not be approached.

It was unclear whether there were other perpetrators. No arrests have been made yet.

Nath said a woman had died at the scene, without providing further details.

Three of the 16 injured had suffered "life-threatening injuries," Nath told reporters.

The city's fire department said eight people were seriously injured, with five sustaining minor injuries.

Nath added that more than 2,200 personnel were involved in the police response, including officers from Hamburg and other federal states.

The vehicle in question is a white minivan or compact SUV, he said.

DW reporters on the scene in Berlin said police officers armed with machine guns were patrolling the streets of the German capital.

Police said early on Sunday morning that the Tiergarten remained closed off.

"We are now piecing together the facts based on the evidence found at the scene. The search radius covers the entire city," Nath said. "We need to use daylight tomorrow to meticulously examine the evidence."

Berlin mayor, Chancellor Merz condemn 'horrific' act

Berlin Mayor Kai Wegner, who visited the scene, described the incident as "an attack on our free and open society."

"After a peaceful and colorful CSD, the assembly for a tolerant and peaceful Berlin was attacked in the most brutal way. Berlin is the city of freedom, and our freedom has been attacked in the most horrific way today," he said on X.

In remarks to reporters at the scene, Wegner said, "We will not allow our way of life and our way of living together to be taken from us."

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz also condemned what he called a "horrific act."

In a statement, Merz said he and Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt would ensure "this horrific act is fully investigated and punished."

Pride parade participants told to 'go home, please'

Hundreds of thousands of people had taken to the streets of Berlin on Saturday to advocate for tolerance and diversity, culminating in concerts at the Brandenburg Gate.

The event was called off around 10:15 p.m., and a band's performance was interrupted. Authorities urged people to "go home, please," and avoid routes through Tiergarten.

The CSD parade ended on 17 June Street, which crosses Berlin's Tiergarten to the Brandenburg Gate. The Gate has been the venue for concerts since Friday.

Berlin's CSD was first held in 1979, making it Germany's oldest Pride event. Its name comes from Christopher Street — the site of the 1969 Stonewall riots in New York City.

CSD has since evolved from a small protest into a major fixture of the city's cultural and political calendar.

Germany's history of car rammings

Germany has seen a number of car rammings at major public events in recent years.

In 2016, a Tunisian-born man drove a truck into a Christmas market in Berlin, killing 12 people, in the deadliest Islamist attack in Germany's postwar history.

In 2024, a man plowed his car into a busy Christmas market in the city of Magdeburg, killing six people and injuring more than 300. The perpetrator was a Saudi-born atheist who held anti-Islamic and far-right beliefs.

Earlier this year, two people were killed after a man drove a car through a crowd in the eastern German city of Leipzig. Investigators treated the incident as a rampage and the suspect, a German national, was remanded to a psychiatric hospital.

Edited by: Zac Crellin

entries.title: WAFCON 2026: What you need to know
entries.summary: Several months after it was supposed to start and with more teams than first planned, WAFCON 2026 is finally set to begin. The hosts want a maiden title while a tournament outsider have one of its best players.
entries.content:
Morocco

WAFCON 2026: What you need to know

July 25, 2026

Several months after it was supposed to start and with more teams than first planned, WAFCON 2026 is finally set to begin. The hosts want a maiden title while a tournament outsider have one of its best players.

What is WAFCON?

The Women's Africa  Cup of Nations is the continental tournament to find the best women's international team in Africa. It has existed in some form since 1991 but the current competition's history really starts in 1998; it has generally been held every two years since then.

Holders Nigeria have won a record 10 titles with only Equatorial Guinea (2012 as hosts) and South Africa (2022) having broken their domination of the tournament.

Originally planned as a 12-team tournament, the African football federation (CAF) added four more teams after qualification. Those four sides had all lost out in the second phase of qualifying but were then reinstated despite CAF earlier denying such changes were afoot. It was a sign of things to come.

Where and when is WAFCON 2026 being played?

For a third successive tournament, WAFCON is to be hosted by Morocco. Specifically, games are to be played in Rabat and Casablanca with a a third city, Fez, dropped from the initial lineup when the fixtures were announced.

Since pulling out of hosting the men's AFCON in 2015, Morocco has become the favored African destination for both CAF and global football's governors FIFA. The North African country, which also hosted the men's AFCON last year, is to cohost the 2030 men's World Cup and has been chosen, or been the sole bidder, for a number of continental and international youth tournaments.

The tournament opener, between Algeria and Senegal, is on July 26, with Morocco opening against Kenya later that day. The final is scheduled for August 16 in Rabat.

Why is WAFCON being played straight after the men's World Cup?

It wasn't supposed to be. After weeks of rumor, denial and a South African offer to step in as hosts, CAF announced just 12 days before the tournament was due to start in March that it would be postponed. CAF, rather vaguely, cited "unforeseen circumstances" as the reason for the delay.

"It is a combination of factors, and it is not a decision taken lightly," Luxolo September, CAF's head of communications, told DW at the time.

"There is a question of the host nation, Morocco, requesting a postponement for a number of reasons. There has been a lot of interaction between Morocco, FIFA and CAF regarding the date. This is not a nice position for us. We have taken no joy from this. We would have loved to play in this window. It is a window we had requested."

Many teams, fans and players were frustrated by the short notice, with preparations made and money shelled out far in advance. It was not the first time though. Two years earlier, the tournament had been postponed by a year because the tournament clashed with the Olympics in Paris — a key date in the women's football calendar.

As well as coming hot on the heels of the men's World Cup, WAFCON 26 will now finish as the season starts in many countries. Germany's women's season for example, kicks off with the first round of the DFB Cup on same weekend as the WAFCON final.

Who are the favorites at WAFCON 26?

Hosts Morocco will want to match their men's side, who won their AFCON tournament in controversial circumstances earlier this year, their maiden title, having lost the previous two finals.

Perennial champions Nigeria will once again enter as favorites while the 2022 winners, South Africa, will also fancy their chances. Below that are a host of teams who could cause a few surprises, including Ivory Coast, Egypt and debutants Cape Verde, whose men's side became one of the stories of the World Cup.

Who are the players to watch at WAFCON 26?

Apart from Zambia's Barbra Banda and Racheal Kundananji, Nigeria's Rasheedat Ajibade may be the most highly regarded talent. Named player of the tournament in 2024, Ajibade is a leader for her team, as well as its sharpest attacking threat. At the other end of the pitch, Nigeria will rely on Chiamaka Nnadozie, regarded as the continent's best goalkeeper.

Hosts Morocco will look to Ghizlaine Chebbak. The top scorer at the last two tournaments, 35-year-old Chebbak may not have too many better chances to win a first major international honor.

Elsewhere, Tabitha Chawinga, of French champions Lyon, will carry the hopes of debutants Malawi, the lowest FIFA-ranked side in the competition. Chawinga's international career has been interrupted by her club commitments but she has an exceptional 25 goals in her 11 caps to date. Her sister, Temwa, is also in the Malawi squad and plays her club football for the Kansas City Current of the NWSL, the top league in the United States. There, she won the 2025 Golden Boot as top goal scorer with 15 goals in 23 games.

Edited by: Chuck Penfold

entries.title: Flavio Bolsonaro gets party nod to run against Brazil's Lula
entries.summary: Flavio Bolsonaro won support from Argentine President Javier Milei and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, though tariffs imposed by Donald Trump's administration could complicate his path to the presidency.
entries.content:
Brazil

Flavio Bolsonaro gets party nod to run against Brazil's Lula

July 25, 2026

Flavio Bolsonaro won support from Argentine President Javier Milei and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, though tariffs imposed by Donald Trump's administration could complicate his path to the presidency.

Flavio Bolsonaro, son of Brazil's former President Jair Bolsonaro, was confirmed Saturday as his father's Liberal Party candidate to challenge incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva.

"Bolsonaro's blood flows here," he declared at the party convention in Sao Paulo.

His father has been sentenced to 27 years in prison for plotting a coup following his loss to Lula in the 2022 election.

Brazil's presidential election is scheduled to be held on October 4. If no candidate wins an outright majority, a runoff will take place on October 25.

Support from Milei and Netanyahu

The younger Bolsonaro still lacks a running mate and centrist backing, while the absence of major political figures at Saturday's party convention highlighted his struggle to build an anti-Lula alliance before October.

He did, however, get support from Argentine President Javier Milei, who endorsed his bid for the presidency.

"I firmly believe there is no one else capable of putting an end to the Lula risk hanging over Brazil," Milei, who attended the party convention, said.

Bolsonaro also showed a short video message of support from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Bolsonaro's campaign faces challenges

He has also developed ties with US conservatives and Donald Trump's administration. In May, he posted pictures he took in the Oval Office with the US president on social media.

The Trump administration has, however, since imposed new tariffs on Brazilian exports of up to 37.5%.

A poll released Friday shows Lula would defeat Flavio Bolsonaro in a potential runoff, 48% to 43%. A June survey showed Lula ahead 47% to 43%.

Lula's left-wing Workers' Party (PT) is expected to formally nominate him as its candidate in August.

Edited by: Rana Taha

entries.title: Serbia's LGBTQ+ community faces 'epidemic of violence'
entries.summary: Documented cases of violence against LGBTQ+ people in Serbia have never been higher. The attacks are part of a larger shift in society targeting marginalized people.
entries.content:
Serbia

Serbia's LGBTQ+ community faces 'epidemic of violence'

July 25, 2026

Documented cases of violence against LGBTQ+ people in Serbia have never been higher. The attacks are part of a larger shift in society targeting marginalized people.

Amid a slew of blows and homophobic insults, the woman on the bus lashed out at Aleksandar Savic and stabbed him with a sharp object. Later, in the emergency room, doctors treated Savic for a cut to the calf and injuries to his eye.

Incidents like the July 11 attack on Savic — also know as drag queen Alexis Plastik — don't happen often in Belgrade. But violence against people who don't look or act like the mainstream in the EU candidate country is becoming increasingly common.

Just a few hours earlier, Vladimir Arsenijevic, author and program director of the annual Krokodil Literary Festival, was attacked in central Belgrade in the middle of the day by right-wing thugs, as he was preparing for a memorial event commemorating the 1995 Srebrenica genocide.

Speaking with broadcaster N1, Plastik called out the "epidemic of violence" in Serbia. The increasing violence by groups associated with President Aleksandar Vucic and his Serbian Progressive Party, SNS, has reinforced the feeling among many people that anyone who is different can become a target, and that no one is safe.

"Violence is becoming increasingly normal, while protection against it is anything but guaranteed — especially for those who speak out against social or political problems, or who are unpopular with the general public," said Matija Stefanovic, the program coordinator for the LGBTQ+ group Da se Zna! ("For Your Information!"), which documents violence against queer people in Serbia.

"The fact that most of these attacks aren't investigated and that the perpetrators are rarely held accountable means they can't be dismissed as isolated incidents," said Stefanovic. "They represent a systemic problem that further stokes violence and emboldens perpetrators to continue attacking marginalized people, without having to fear significant consequences."

The social climate has become decidedly harsher for Serbia's LGBTQ+ community over the last few years, with the community also increasingly the target of right-wing nationalist government.

More recorded attacks than ever before

Da se Zna! is based in an unassuming office on a side street in the center of the Serbian capital. Aside from a lone rainbow-colored nutcracker standing on a shelf, hardly anything indicates the group's purpose: it's the only organization in Serbia to document attacks on queer people — threats, vandalism, physical assault.

"Last year, we counted 110 cases — more than ever before," said Stefanovic. That's due in part to the fact that the NGO is becoming more well-known, and queer people are increasingly ready to report incidents. But dramatic, high-profile cases like the aggression against Alexis Plastik are also happening more and more.

In mid-May, unknown assailants attacked Mornar, a queer bar in Belgrade, with tear gas. At the end of May, a trans woman and her partner were beaten unconscious one night — again, by unidentified attackers.

Many queer people in Serbia are scared of openly showing their identity. In a recent survey by the European Union Agency for Fundamental Rights, some 80% of respondents said they avoided holding the hand of their partner in public.

The latest edition of the Rainbow Map, compiled by the International Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Trans and Intersex Association, shows that Serbia has slipped to 29th place in Europe, six spots below the European average. Five years ago, it was in 22nd place.

Support amid threats of violence

The only solution to this stigmatization and violence is education, said Stefanovic. Next to the yearly Pride parade co-organized by Da se Zna!, activists also travel to small towns around the country with a Pride Caravan to send a message: we're here, and we're not going anywhere.

In some of the towns, they're greeted by a handful of supporters holding rainbow flags — and dozens of demonstrators shouting homophobic slogans.

After the group published a list of the planned destinations for this year's caravan, they received several death threats. The event in Pirot, in Serbia's southeast, was called off on short notice in mid-July because police could not guarantee the group's safety. Three journalists covering the event were attacked by the mob.

"These protests show the sad reality for queer people living in a small Serbian town," said Stefanovic. "We try to show the people living in these towns that we know how hard it is — and that we haven't forgotten about them."

Struggle to live openly in a small town

Stefanovic knows exactly how it feels to grow up queer in a small town far from the cosmopolitan city of Belgrade.

"I wanted to be a boy for as long as I can remember. Every night I prayed to God that he would turn me into one," he told DW.

Only as a teenager did Stefanovic learn about other people that felt like him — and that they were known as trans. But this knowledge did nothing to ease his worries.

"Once I realized [who I was,] I felt the weight of everything I would have to go through as a result," he said.

It was only when Stefanovic moved to Belgrade for his studies that he felt free enough to openly live as Matija. He came out as trans, first to several professors at the university, then to friends. Finally, one day, he wrote to his parents, an eight-page letter in which he explained everything that had preoccupied him for years.

Stefanovic then made two life-changing decisions: he began hormone treatment to align his biological sex with his gender identity — and he did so openly. At the time, there were very few people living openly as trans in Serbia, and not much information was available on how to undergo gender-affirming treatment.

"It sounds totally cliche, but I wanted to become the person that I needed in my life when I first exploring my own gender identify," said Stefanovic. He filmed his transition, first putting his videos on YouTube and then on TikTok.

TV interviews followed soon after — and the attention of right-wing groups on Facebook. At first, the hate directed toward Stefanovic seemed unbearable. But he decided to keep going, to stay visible, so that trans people would someday belong.

Stefanovic knows that acceptance is a process, and that people can change their views. His family is a prime example — his conservative father was the first person to consistently use the right pronoun and new name. And last year, both his parents took part in Belgrade's Pride parade for the first time.

"I'm so proud of them," said Stefanovic. "My parents have become my greatest allies."

This article was originally written in German.
